        INTERVENOR BKV LAND HOLDINGS I, LLC POST-HEARING REPLY BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE:
       BKV Land Holdings I, LLC (“BKV”) ﬁles the following post-hearing reply brief and in
support would show the following.

                                I.   INTRODUCTION

       The Commission’s task in this proceeding is not to identify a perfect route—none
exists—but to select the route that best satisﬁes the routing criteria under PURA § PQ.RST(c)
and UT TAC § VS.URU(b)(P)(B) based on the evidentiary record. On that record, the answer is
clear. Route YZ[ is the only route that consistently performs well across the Commission’s
primary criteria while avoiding severe, site-speciﬁc conﬂicts with existing and planned land
uses. It is among the shortest and least expensive alternatives, minimizes impacts to
habitable structures, parallels existing rights-of-way and property boundaries for a




                                             1
 substantial portion of its length, and avoids creating unique or disproportionate land use
conﬂicts.1

           This conclusion is conﬁrmed when Route 894 is compared to any route incorporating
Link A42. Every such route performs worse on the Commission’s core criteria and introduces
a fatal, site-speciﬁc conﬂict that the applicants failed to account for in route development—
namely, the destruction of BKV’s integrated data center and generation project. Unlike
generalized land-use impacts that can be mitigated or accommodated, this conﬂict is
binary: the transmission line and BKV’s project cannot coexist on the same property.2
           Several parties assert that Route 894 adversely agects agricultural, ranching,
hunting, and rural land uses.3 But the record demonstrates that these concerns are
overstated and, more importantly, legally insugicient to displace Route 894. Across Texas,
these uses routinely coexist with transmission infrastructure.4 By contrast, the impacts
associated with Link A[V are not matters of degree—they are categorically incompatible with
BKV’s project and therefore weigh far more heavily under the Commission’s land-use
compatibility analysis.
           Although certain Link A42 routes are nominally less expensive, those same routes
impose substantially greater impacts to habitable structures, a factor the Commission has
repeatedly treated as paramount. Commission Stag itself recommended Route 487 over
cheaper alternatives for precisely this reason.5 The same logic applies here: cost digerences
cannot justify materially greater impacts to residences, particularly where those cost
estimates are unreliable. Here, the applicants’ estimates fail to account for BKV’s actual use

2

                                                           2
 of the property and the resulting increase in land and right-of-way acquisition costs.6 When
properly considered, routes incorporating Link A42 would likely be more expensive than

Route 894, eliminating any asserted cost advantage.
           Notably, the applicants did not evaluate or incorporate BKV’s project in developing
the alternative routes at issue.7 As a result, the record shows that routes incorporating
Link A42 were never meaningfully vetted against existing land uses, undermining their
reliability under the Commission’s routing criteria. This omission further distinguishes Route
894 as the only route supported by a complete and accurate assessment of real-world
impacts.

                                II.    SOLAR GENERATION FACILITY

           Arguments that routes incorporating Link AV are not viable due to impacts on a solar
generation facility are unsupported by the record and mischaracterize the applicants’
evidence. The impacts to that facility were fully identiﬁed, quantiﬁed, and agirmatively
accepted by both the applicants and Commission Stag in developing and recommending
their respective preferred routes.8 Every other expert ogering a recommendation on the route
has done the same and recommended a route that uses Link AV.9
           Mr. Burnett’s reliance on Mr. Marusak’s testimony is misplaced. Mr. Marusak did not
testify that removal of solar infrastructure renders a route unsuitable. Rather, in context, his
testimony conﬁrmed only that the underlying data in the environmental assessment remains

at 4.
7
 BKV Ex. 4 (Applicants’ Supplemental Response to BKV’s First Requests for Information, Interrogatory No. 1-4)
at 4; Tr. (Vol. 2) at 28:10–12, 28:24–29:1, 30:11, 30:14–17, 31:7 (Marusak Cross) (Jun. 8, 2026); Tr. (Vol. 2) at 29:4–

 E.g., Applicants Ex. 1 (Joint Application) at Attachment No. 1 (Environmental Assessment) at 3-91 (Bates 176),
7-26 (Bates 247), Appendix G (Environmental and Land Use Constraints Maps) at Figure 3-1A (Bates 1822);
Applicants Ex. 2 (Cooley Direct) at 21:5–10; Commission StaK Ex. 1 (Poole Direct) at 17:19–18:5; Tr. (Vol. 4)
at 140:15–19; 155:8–10; 168:21–25; 212:15–18 (Poole Cross) (Jun. 10, 2026).
9
    E.g., Colorado River Alliance Intervenors Ex. CRAI-1 (Buntz Direct) at 7:13–18.

 reliable. Mr. Burnett supports his argument by mischaracterizing testimony from
Mr. Marusak and arguing that Link AV “would do exactly what Mr. Marusak said he could not

imagine generally happening. It would rip out existing solar generation.”10 But this was not
Mr. Marusak’s testimony. At the hearing on the merits, Mr. Burnett asked Mr. Marusak
whether he would agree that the number of solar generation facilities located within Bell,
Coryell, and Menard Counties has not decreased since VRVP (that is, whether the applicants’
information, which cited to sources from VRVP, was still reliable11). In response, Mr. Marusak
simply stated, “Yes. It certainly would not go down. I can’t imagine them ripping them out.”12
           Nothing in Mr. Marusak’s testimony supports elevating solar facility impacts above
the Commission’s broader balancing of routing criteria. To the contrary, the applicants have
continued to support a Route YZ[ conﬁguration—with full knowledge of those impacts—
because it best balances competing considerations.13

                                           III.    CONCLUSION

           Commission precedent conﬁrms that impacts to generation facilities—including
solar facilities—do not preclude route selection where, as here, the overall balance of
factors supports that route.14 The undisputed record shows that every routing expert to oger
a recommendation—including the applicants and Commission stag—did so with full
awareness of the solar impacts and nevertheless recommended routes utilizing Link A2.
There is no evidentiary basis to treat those impacts as disqualifying in this proceeding.

aKect more homes, increase length and ineKiciency, or impact landowners”).


                                                           4
        The evidentiary record leads to a straightforward conclusion: Route 894 is the only
route that reasonably satisﬁes the Commission’s statutory and regulatory criteria without

introducing disproportionate or irreconcilable land-use conﬂicts. Routes incorporating
Link A42 are inferior based on the Commission’s primary factors and are independently
ﬂawed by their incompatibility with BKV’s project and the applicants’ failure to account for
that impact.
       BKV respectfully requests that the Administrative Law Judges recommend, and the
Commission approve, Route 894 as the best-meets route. In the alternative, and consistent
with Commission Stag’s analysis, Route 487 is also supported by the record.


                                   Respectfully submitted,
